```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

[taxonAlign](https://github.com/traitecoevo/taxonAlign) aligns raw taxon names against a taxonomic
reference in its own reference format (see `taxonAlign::taxonomic_reference_schema()`). Most users
never need anything else: taxonAlign's `load_taxonomic_resources()` downloads ready-made references
from a dated data release.

`taxonAlign.dataprep` is for when you need to build a reference yourself. It:

- reshapes particular sources into taxonAlign's format: the Australian National Species List
  exports, including the Australian Faunal Directory's (`load_NSL()`), the Australian Plant
  Census (`load_APC()`), and two worldwide checklists, the World Checklist of Vascular Plants
  (`load_WCVP()`) and the Catalogue of Life (`load_CoL()`);
- builds a reference from the GBIF backbone taxonomy, live (`generate_GBIF_taxonomic_reference_list()`)
  or from a [taxadb](https://docs.ropensci.org/taxadb/) snapshot
  (`generate_taxadb_taxonomic_reference_list()`);
- walks you through turning your own reference tables into the format (`build_taxonomic_reference()`);
- builds the data releases taxonAlign downloads (`data-raw/build_data_release.R`).

Every function returns one table in taxonAlign's format, which can go straight into taxonAlign's
matching functions, alone or combined with other references.

```{r setup}
library(taxonAlign.dataprep)
library(taxonAlign)
```

## Your own reference tables

If you have a taxonomic reference table -- your own species list, an export from a museum database,
whatever -- with its own column names, `build_taxonomic_reference()` maps it onto taxonAlign's
format. Columns it recognises (taxonAlign's own names, or the Darwin Core ones, such as
`canonicalName`, `taxonRank`) are picked up automatically; for each required column that's still
missing you're asked (in the style of `traits.build`'s `metadata_add_traits()`) to pick one of the
table's columns, or to give a fixed value. Then it asks whether you have any further references to
add, as many as you like, and, if there's more than one, their priority order:

```{r}
#| eval: false
my_reference <- build_taxonomic_reference()
#> Enter the file path for your taxonomic reference: my_beetles.csv
#> Does the data have a column for `taxon_rank`, or is every row the same value? ...
#> ... (column mapping for my_beetles.csv) ...
#> Do you have any additional taxonomic reference(s) to include? 1: Yes 2: No
#> Selection: 1
#> Enter the file path for the additional taxonomic reference: more_beetles.csv
#> ... (column mapping for more_beetles.csv) ...
#> Do you have any additional taxonomic reference(s) to include? 1: Yes 2: No
#> Selection: 2
#> Multiple taxonomic reference tables were supplied. Enter their priority order ...
```

The result is one table, combined in that priority order. Save it, check it, and use it:

```{r}
#| eval: false
readr::write_csv(my_reference, "my_reference.csv")
check_taxonomic_reference(my_reference)
create_taxonomic_update_lookup(c("Xylotoles costatus", "Xylotoles sp. 1"), my_reference)
```

See `?build_taxonomic_reference` for the full set of prompts, and for supplying the answers in a
script instead.

## From the GBIF backbone taxonomy

`generate_GBIF_taxonomic_reference_list()` builds a reference from the GBIF backbone taxonomy for any
taxon name, optionally restricted to a country and/or a minimum rank. The whole subtree is fetched
once and cached, so repeat calls are fast.

```{r}
aporocera <- generate_GBIF_taxonomic_reference_list("Aporocera", country = "AU")
create_taxonomic_update_lookup(c("Aporocera viridipennis", "Aporocera viridipenis", "Aporocera sp. 1"), aporocera)
```

Real GBIF data can include a handful of "doubtful" or incompletely-classified records with no
canonical name at all (the backbone also holds BOLD Barcode Index Numbers as unranked "taxa", named
like `"BOLD:AAX6343"`) -- taxonAlign drops these automatically (with a warning), since a name with no
usable label could never be matched against anyway.

GBIF's occurrence records include fossil specimens, so a `country` filter would otherwise keep fossil
taxa. Taxa GBIF flags as extinct, and their synonyms, are left out by default
(`exclude_extinct = TRUE`); that includes recently extinct species (the thylacine is flagged extinct
too), and `exclude_extinct = FALSE` keeps them, with an `extinct` column. For all Australian animals at
once, use the released list (`taxonAlign::load_taxonomic_resources("GBIF_AU")`) rather than building
it live, which takes many hours.

## From taxadb (a pre-cached snapshot of GBIF, ITIS, and others)

`generate_GBIF_taxonomic_reference_list()` fetches live from GBIF's API -- practical for a small
clade, but slow for a genuinely large one (a phylum, a large class). For a large group,
`generate_taxadb_taxonomic_reference_list()` instead sources from
[taxadb](https://docs.ropensci.org/taxadb/)'s own pre-built, locally-cached snapshot -- fast
regardless of size, at the cost of the snapshot possibly being out of date (check
`taxadb:::available_versions()` to see how current it is before relying on it for anything
time-sensitive, or pass `gbif_snapshot_url` to query a current GBIF snapshot directly):

```{r}
#| eval: false
# every taxon in the class Insecta that taxadb's GBIF snapshot has
insecta <- generate_taxadb_taxonomic_reference_list("Insecta", rank = "class", provider = "gbif")

# the same, restricted to taxa with an Australian GBIF occurrence record
insecta_au <- generate_taxadb_taxonomic_reference_list(
  "Insecta", rank = "class", provider = "gbif", country = "AU"
)
```

Unlike `generate_GBIF_taxonomic_reference_list()`, `rank` here is required -- it tells the function
which column (`kingdom`/`phylum`/`class`/`order`/`family`/`genus`) to filter on, since taxadb has no
single "fetch below this name" concept the way a live GBIF fetch does. `taxadb` is only needed for this
function, so it's a suggested rather than a required dependency: install it with
`install.packages("taxadb")` if you use it.

## From the National Species List and the APC

`load_NSL()` reshapes one group's National Species List export -- `"animals"` (the Australian Faunal
Directory's NSL export), `"algae"`, `"bryophytes"`, `"fungi"` or `"lichens"`. Each group is a pair of
files: the *taxon* file (accepted names and their synonyms, with links between them) and the *names*
file (every name recorded for the group). By default `load_NSL()` reads the verbatim copies of both
stored in a taxonAlign data release -- this is exactly how the release's ready-to-use list is built --
so, like `taxonAlign::load_taxonomic_resources()`, it needs no file of your own, and `version` names the
release:

```{r}
#| eval: false
bryophytes <- load_NSL("bryophytes", version = "2026-10-07")
```

For an export you've downloaded yourself, from the group's NSL export page (e.g.
`https://fungi.biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/export/index`), point `path` at the folder holding its
two files:

```{r}
#| eval: false
fungi_now <- load_NSL("fungi", path = "my_downloads/fungi_export")
```

`load_APC()` loads the Australian Plant Census, via `APCalign::load_taxonomic_resources()`, which
downloads and caches APC releases itself:

```{r}
#| eval: false
apc <- load_APC()
```

`vignettes/AFD-data-processing.qmd` records every transformation `load_NSL()` makes to the AFD's NSL
export, with counts, and how it compared with the AFD's own CSV export format.

## Worldwide checklists: the WCVP and the Catalogue of Life

`load_WCVP()` loads the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew), every vascular
plant name worldwide (~1.45 million), and `load_CoL()` the Catalogue of Life, a reference to every
taxon in every kingdom (~5.5 million names), from [ChecklistBank](https://api.checklistbank.org). The first call
downloads the source (~90MB and ~170MB); both the download and the reshaped table are cached, so every
later call loads from your computer, offline. Without a version, the first call gets the current WCVP
or the latest COL release, and later calls keep using that one -- `refresh_cache = TRUE` checks for a
newer one:

```{r}
#| eval: false
wcvp <- load_WCVP()                       # first time: downloads the current version
wcvp <- load_WCVP()                       # later: the same version, from the cache
wcvp <- load_WCVP(refresh_cache = TRUE)   # check Kew for a newer version
```

Both can be pinned, so an alignment can be repeated exactly. The WCVP by version number:

```{r}
#| eval: false
wcvp <- load_WCVP(16)
attr(wcvp, "citation")
```

The Catalogue of Life by a release's ChecklistBank key (`316595` is COL26.10, `310463` the COL25
annual release) or alias. The default, `"3LR"`, is the latest release;
`https://api.checklistbank.org/dataset?releasedFrom=3&origin=release` lists them all:

```{r}
#| eval: false
col <- load_CoL(316595)
attr(col, "doi")
```

The first load is slow (the COL especially: a ~170MB download and ~5.5 million names to reshape),
and so is preparing a list that size for matching. If you'll align more than one list, prepare it
once and reuse it, rather than passing the raw table to each call; restricting it to a country first
(below) also makes it far smaller:

```{r}
#| eval: false
col_resources <- prepare_taxonomic_resources(col)
lookup_1 <- create_taxonomic_update_lookup(names_1, col_resources)
lookup_2 <- create_taxonomic_update_lookup(names_2, col_resources)
```

Kew's and COL's own statuses are kept (`"illegitimate"`, `"ambiguous synonym"`, ...), except that
COL's `"provisionally accepted"` names become `"accepted"`, since they're the accepted names of their
taxa. See `?load_WCVP` and `?load_CoL` for exactly how each is reshaped.

## Restricting a worldwide list to a country

A worldwide list matches more names than you may want: an Australian plant list aligned against the
whole WCVP can fuzzy-match a misspelt name to a species that only grows in South America.
`filter_to_country()` keeps only the taxa GBIF has occurrence records of in one or more countries:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# first time: downloads the WCVP from Kew, and the names GBIF has records of in Australia
wcvp_au <- load_WCVP() |> filter_to_country("AU")

lookup <- create_taxonomic_update_lookup(my_plant_names, wcvp_au)
```

The two taxonomies don't have to agree. Each name GBIF's Australian records are identified to is
matched to the WCVP's names, accepted or synonym; either way, the WCVP's *accepted* name is kept,
together with all of its synonyms, so an old name in your list still updates. GBIF's Australian
records, for example, include *Polypompholyx multifida*, which the WCVP treats as a synonym of
*Utricularia multifida*: so *Utricularia multifida* is kept, with *Polypompholyx multifida* and every
other synonym of it. Of the 52,330 species-level names in GBIF's Australian vascular plant records
(October 2026), 50,653 matched a WCVP name; the rest are mostly spelling variants and informal names. By default every subspecies and
variety of a kept species is kept too (`whole_species = TRUE`). Genera of the kept species stay, so a
name only identifiable to genus still aligns, and families and other higher ranks are kept whole.

The same works for the Catalogue of Life, and for several countries at once. For a WCVP list, GBIF's
search is limited to vascular plants automatically; for others, name the GBIF group(s) with
`gbif_taxon` to keep the search to the relevant part of GBIF:

```{r}
#| eval: false
col_au_nz <- load_CoL() |>
  filter_to_country(c("AU", "NZ"), gbif_taxon = c("Animalia", "Plantae", "Fungi"))
```

GBIF's names are fetched once per country (one facet query, then GBIF's name parser) and cached, like
the downloads above. `attr(wcvp_au, "unmatched")` lists the names GBIF has records of in the country
that matched nothing in the reference -- names it lacks, or spells differently -- which is worth a look.

GBIF's records include cultivated, introduced and, for animals, fossil occurrences as well as native
ones. Any GBIF occurrence filter can be passed through to narrow them, e.g. only preserved specimens:

```{r}
#| eval: false
wcvp_au_specimens <- load_WCVP() |> filter_to_country("AU", basisOfRecord = "PRESERVED_SPECIMEN")
```

## Combining references

Every function above returns one table, so references combine the way taxonAlign combines any
tables: in a list, most preferred first. Released lists can be mixed in too:

```{r}
#| eval: false
resources <- prepare_taxonomic_resources(c(
  list(mine = my_reference, fungi_now = fungi_now),
  load_taxonomic_resources("GBIF_AU")
))
```

## Building a data release

The data releases taxonAlign downloads are built by `data-raw/build_data_release.R`. For every
dataset, a release holds the source exports exactly as supplied (every column as text), the dataset
in taxonAlign's format (`<dataset>.parquet`, checked with `taxonAlign::check_taxonomic_reference()`),
and a `manifest.csv` recording each file's source, retrieval date, row count, checksum, licence and
citation. taxonAlign only ever downloads the ready files, and learns from the manifest which datasets a
release has -- so adding a dataset needs a new data release, not a new version of taxonAlign. See the
script's header for how to run it and publish the result.
